newsitem.title: UK: Buba gets vocal, froth comes off convergence trades.
newsitem.headline: Buba gets vocal, froth comes off convergence trades.

text.p: The Bundesbank's warnings of the dangers of fiscal window-dressing in the run-up to monetary union has dampened the market's ardour for EMU convergence trades, financial analysts said on Monday.
The German central bank's admonitions have also taken the shine off non-core European currencies and bond markets.

Convergence trades, which speculate that the economies and financial instruments of candidates for European economic and monetary union (EMU) will converge successfully, began shortly after French budget details in September.

They have gradually gathered pace ever since, with substantial gains on the Italian and Spanish bond markets as well as the lira and the peseta. Other non-core markets such as Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Portugal have also done well.

This has mainly been due to the belief that a broad-based union will go ahead in 1999 but it is also being helped by the economically beneficial impact of the fiscal masochism that is taking place in order to qualify for EMU.

"We do not believe that the correction on the EMS crosses signals a more prolonged period of divergence," said Paul Meggyesi, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "It probably does, however, signal an end to the convergence euphoria which has dominated European bond and forex markets over the last few weeks."

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing told reporters on Thursday that fiscal window dressing for EMU "must not happen" and backed up Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer's comments on Wednesday that the central bank was concerned about creative accounting to alter budgetary positions.
Analysts said it was no surprise that the fiercely independent Bundesbank is voicing caution given the current enthusiastic attitude to monetary union among governments.

Despite its independence, the Bundesbank has been stung before when it was overruled by the administration over the one-to-one conversion of ostmarks for deutschemarks when the Berlin Wall came down in late 1989.
It was then left to pick up the inflationary pieces of the exchange and will be keen to see that the credibiliy of the euro is not watered down by budgetary fudges.

"We can look forward to more of this kind of thing from the Bundesbank," said Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC Markets. "While they have been saying such things for some time the market has used it as an excuse to take profits." "The Bundesbank was proved right over the economic impact of German unification and that should, in theory give them more credibility and more clout this time around." The Bundesbank is also keen that the fiscal stability pact -- designed to stop countries allowing their budgets to slip after EMU -- contains automatic sanctions.

EU ministers have already agreed on a pact in principle but nothing is written in stone so the Bundesbank can be expected to push hard for a stability pact with teeth, strict interpretation of the convergence critera and budgets brought under control without any accounting slights of hand.
"The high yielders could thus be faced with an increasingly less friendly political environment and some further squaring of convergence trades is to be expected," Deutsche's Meggyesi said.

If the Bundesbank, and other other core members, do succeed in riding roughshod over the Herculean efforts being made by the non-core European countries, fiscal positions may deteriorate, analysts warned.
